title: Marked simplex and spine extension inclusions
statement:
Use marked simplicial sets, sharp marking, and marked coanodyne maps from [def-coef-infinity-marked-coanodyne]. For $n\geq1$, let $I^n\subseteq\Delta^n$ be the simplicial spine, the union of the consecutive edges $\Delta^{\{i-1,i\}}$ for $1\leq i\leq n$, and put $I^0=\Delta^0$. The two marked inclusions
$$\{0\}^\sharp\longrightarrow(\Delta^n)^\sharp,\qquad (I^n)^\sharp\longrightarrow(\Delta^n)^\sharp$$
are marked coanodyne for every $n\geq0$. Consequently, if a marked map $q:X\to Y$ has the right lifting property against marked coanodyne maps, either inclusion $j:U\hookrightarrow(\Delta^n)^\sharp$ has the following relative parameter extension property: for any monomorphism $T\hookrightarrow T'$ of simplicial sets, marked maps from $((\Delta^n)^\sharp\times T^\flat)\amalg_{U\times T^\flat}(U\times(T')^\flat)$ to $X$ over a prescribed marked map $(\Delta^n)^\sharp\times(T')^\flat\to Y$ extend to $(\Delta^n)^\sharp\times(T')^\flat$. The parameter may be empty and its prescribed data may be an entire boundary, not just a horn.

source.place: Agent combinatorial consequence of HTT Definition 3.1.1.1 (opposite marked horn and triangle generators), with the relative parameter clause given by Proposition 3.1.2.3 under opposite reversal. The explicit subset/horn filtration is recorded in the second-reading report; Corollary 2.3.2.5 is an exponentiation result and is not cited as a spine-filtration theorem. Read directly in the IAS PDF. No Stacks tag states this marked assertion.

proof.text: For $n=0$ both maps are identities. For $n\geq1$, start with the marked vertex $\{0\}^\sharp$ and, successively for $r=1,\ldots,n$, attach the fully marked edge $\Delta^{\{r-1,r\}}$ at its source vertex $r-1$. The intersection of this edge with the earlier edges is exactly that source vertex. Each attachment is a pushout of generator (ii) of [def-coef-infinity-marked-coanodyne] in dimension $1$, since $\Lambda^1_0=\{0\}$ and the initial edge is the whole edge. The resulting marked union is $(I^n)^\sharp$. Closure under finite compositions therefore proves $\{0\}^\sharp\to(I^n)^\sharp$ marked coanodyne.

source.place: Definition 3.1.1.1(2), opposite reversal; explicit successive edge attachments.

proof.text: We now give a finite filtration of the spine inclusion, without assuming a spine-extension theorem. By the simplex description in [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones], the nondegenerate simplices of $\Delta^n$ correspond exactly to nonempty subsets of $\{0,\ldots,n\}$: an increasing map factors uniquely as its surjection onto its image followed by that increasing image inclusion, and precomposition with a surjection is a degeneracy. Write $\Delta^U$ for the face with vertex set $U$. The subsets already in $I^n$ are the singletons and the consecutive pairs. Every remaining subset belongs to exactly one pair $(S,U)$ with $a=\min S$, $b=\max S$, $b-a\geq2$, $a+1\notin S$, and $U=S\cup\{a+1\}$. Indeed a remaining subset lacking its second possible vertex is $S$, while one containing it is $U$, with $S$ recovered by deleting that vertex. Order these finitely many pairs by increasing $b-a$, then increasing $|S|$, and then lexicographically to break ties.

source.place: Definition 3.1.0.1 and Definition 3.1.1.1(1),(3); agent subset filtration, pairing and ordering.

proof.text: For each pair in step 2, the intersection of $\Delta^U$ with the preceding union is exactly the inner horn that omits the face $\Delta^S$. Here $a+1$ is the second vertex of $U$, so the horn index is $1$ and its dimension is $m=|U|-1\geq2$. To check the other codimension-one faces: deleting $a$ or $b$ decreases the interval length, unless the result is already a singleton or consecutive pair in the spine; deleting any other vertex except $a+1$ leaves an upper member of a pair with the same endpoints and smaller $|S|$. These faces are therefore present. Conversely neither $S$ nor $U$ is present: if an earlier upper member contained $S$, its interval would contain $[a,b]$ and hence could not have smaller length. Equal length forces the same endpoints, and containing $S$ then forces at least $|S|$ vertices in its lower member, with equality only for this very pair. Thus no earlier pair supplies either simplex. Every proper subset of $S$ is contained in one of the other codimension-one faces of $U$, so the intersection is the whole horn and nothing more. This uses exactly the horn-as-union-of-faces definition of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones].

source.place: Definition 3.1.1.1(1); agent subset filtration, verification of the exact attaching horn.

proof.text: Keep the preceding union fully marked. Attach $\Delta^U$ by pushing out the flat inner-horn generator (i) of [def-coef-infinity-marked-coanodyne] along the horn of step 3. This adds precisely the underlying simplices $S,U$ and preserves all existing marked edges. If $m\geq3$, every edge of $\Delta^U$ already belongs to its horn, so all its edges are marked and the new union is fully marked. If $m=2$, the vertices are $a,a+1,b$; the horn consists of its two consecutive edges, which were both already marked, and the newly adjoined edge $\{a,b\}$ is initially unmarked. Push out generator (iii) along this triangle to mark that edge, without changing the underlying simplicial set. Thus in both cases the inclusion of fully marked unions is a composite of marked coanodyne maps. The pairs exhaust all simplices outside the spine, so finite composition proves $(I^n)^\sharp\to(\Delta^n)^\sharp$ marked coanodyne. Compose with step 1 to prove the initial-vertex inclusion as well. This also covers $n=1$, when the spine filtration is empty.

source.place: Definition 3.1.1.1(1),(3), opposite reversal; agent filtration, marking audit and finite composition.

proof.text: To apply the existing marked-anodyne theorem with the correct variance, define $X^{\mathrm{op}}$ by reversing the order on every simplex: an operator $\alpha:[r]\to[s]$ is replaced by $i\mapsto s-\alpha(r-i)$. Applying this operation twice is the identity; it preserves degreewise products and pushouts and sends markings to the reversed edges. It takes $\Lambda_i^m$ to $\Lambda_{m-i}^m$, so a Kan complex remains Kan. Comparing the four generators in [def-coef-infinity-marked-coanodyne] with the four generators in [lem-coef-marked-anodyne-lifting-calculus], it exchanges the initial and final marked horn generators, preserves the inner-horn family, preserves the triangle marking generator (the two consecutive edges are interchanged), and takes the Kan marking generators to Kan marking generators. It preserves the stated closure operations and is involutive. Consequently a map is marked coanodyne exactly when its opposite is marked anodyne.

source.place: Definition 3.1.1.1 and Remark 3.1.1.2; direct comparison of generators under opposite reversal.

proof.text: Let $D=(\Delta^n)^\sharp$, let $j:U\to D$ be either inclusion, and let $i:T\hookrightarrow T\prime$ be the given monomorphism. The map $i^\flat:T^\flat\to(T\prime)^\flat$ is degreewise injective, hence so is its opposite. By steps 4-5, $j^{\mathrm{op}}$ is marked anodyne. Apply the pushout-product assertion of [lem-coef-marked-anodyne-lifting-calculus] to $j^{\mathrm{op}}$ and $(i^\flat)^{\mathrm{op}}$. The result is marked anodyne. Reversing again, using the products and pushouts checked in step 5, shows that $(D\times T^\flat)\amalg_{U\times T^\flat}(U\times(T\prime)^\flat)\to D\times(T\prime)^\flat$ is marked coanodyne. The prescribed data are exactly a commutative lifting square against this map and $q$. The assumed right lifting property supplies a marked diagonal over the specified map to $Y$, which is the requested relative extension. No nonemptiness or horn condition on $T\hookrightarrow T\prime$ was used: $T=\varnothing$, $T=\partial\Delta^r$ (including $r=0$), and $T=T\prime$ are included.

source.place: Proposition 3.1.2.3, opposite reversal, and the assumed right lifting property.
